routes.description: Establish perfect-mind theism as the preferable foundational hypothesis by comparing its commitments and its expectations for the observed universe with those of non-theistic and rival-origin hypotheses.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a perfect mind is sufficiently coherent as an origin hypothesis, carries a comparative simplicity advantage, and makes the relevant observations sufficiently more expected to justify preferring it over non-theism.

motionBridge.description: Connect comparative simplicity and differential expectedness to the conclusion that a perfect mind created the universe and is favored over non-theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that every worldview bears foundational commitments and that a perfect foundational mind requires fewer or less arbitrary commitments than its competitors.
Show that moral agency, beauty, fine-tuning, meaning, purpose, and related observations are more probable under a perfect-mind hypothesis than under an indifferent foundation.
Supply a principled connection between the attributes of a perfect mind and its expected production of a universe containing the cited observations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Justify comparative support rather than conclusive demonstration as the appropriate epistemic standard for choosing among foundational hypotheses.
Explain how hiddenness, suffering, disagreement, and imperfect conditions bear on but do not erase the claimed evidential contribution of favorable observations.

routes.description: Defeat preference for perfect-mind theism by requiring an identifiable creator hypothesis, justified comparative probabilities, and explanatory connections that distinguish it from naturalistic and supernatural rivals.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the perfect-mind hypothesis remains undefined or underdetermined, its likelihood comparisons lack a justified basis, or the complete evidential profile fails to favor it over non-theistic alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that compatibility with selected observations does not establish or preferentially support a perfect mind as the creator of the universe.

centralBridges.description: Require a coherent means to establish that a perfect mind is possible, identifiable, detectable, capable of creation, and causally responsible for this universe.
Require specified hypotheses and a justified comparison class before assigning greater probability to the observed features under theism than under non-theism.
Require an intelligible account of how or why the proposed mind produces the observations and how that account differs from mere compatibility or accommodation.
Account for the cited observations through interacting, adapted, and fallible agents while testing theism against rival supernatural hypotheses and contrary evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Determine whether introducing a highly capable perfect mind and auxiliary claims is genuinely simpler than withholding that additional ontological commitment.
Test the expectations of moral perfection against divine hiddenness, moral disagreement, suffering, absent correction, and the universe's imperfect conditions.

sections.title: Perfect-Mind Coherence, Identification, and Causal Burden
sections.rationale: This issue determines what must be established about a perfect mind before observations can support the claim that such a being exists, created the universe, and is distinguishable from nearby rival origins.

sections.title: Foundational Commitments and Comparative Simplicity
sections.rationale: This issue compares whether theism and non-theism carry equivalent foundational burdens and whether perfection reduces commitments or instead introduces an additional complex, underdetermined entity.

sections.title: Comparative Likelihood and Evidential Method
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether differential expectedness can provide support without conclusive demonstration and whether the relevant conditional probabilities and comparison classes can be justified.

sections.title: Explanatory Power and Rival Accounts of Observed Features
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether moral agency, beauty, fine-tuning, meaning, and purpose receive a distinctive explanatory connection to a perfect mind or are comparably accounted for by agents and rival hypotheses.

sections.title: Divine Attributes, Hiddenness, and Contrary Expectations
sections.rationale: This issue evaluates how moral perfection and creative intention bear on expected disclosure, moral guidance, suffering, disagreement, and imperfection, including proposed goods served by limited disclosure.

routes.description: Establish theism as a legitimate personal explanation whose simplicity and divine purposes make the universe's order, consciousness, moral agency, and associated general features more probable than they would be without God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent personal-explanation framework, connects simplicity to prior probability, derives relevant expectations from the proposed divine nature, and accounts for apparent counterevidence without losing the comparative explanatory inference.

motionBridge.description: Show that a simple divine-agent hypothesis makes the universe and its general features sufficiently more expected than relevant non-theistic alternatives to count as the most probable explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish purposive personal causation as a genuine and applicable explanatory mode alongside explanation through physical states and laws.
Justify simplicity as a basis for assigning prior probability while retaining evidential fit and predictive accuracy as constraints on hypothesis choice.
Derive reasons for a perfectly good and powerful God to create an orderly, life-producing universe containing conscious agents with consequential freedom.
Reconcile grave suffering and other apparent tensions with the proposed divine nature through morally relevant opportunity, obligations toward sufferers, or compensating goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify how economy in entities, properties, and mathematical structure operates in ordinary explanatory and scientific comparisons.
Connect regular natural laws and embodied conditions to the possibility of rational consciousness, purposive action, and morally significant choice.

routes.description: Deny that the proposed divine hypothesis earns the claimed comparative probability by challenging its explanatory category, simplicity, predictive specificity, coherence, and ability to accommodate suffering and human nature.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more indispensable links from divine simplicity to explanatory probability fails, or if the hypothesis remains insufficiently discriminating, internally strained, or poorly aligned with major features it is offered to explain.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available general features do not warrant treating God as the simplest and most probable explanation because the proposed comparison lacks a justified or adequately predictive basis.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the exhaustiveness or applicability of the division between inanimate causal explanation and purposive personal explanation.
Show that competing notions of simplicity can diverge and that an infinite, qualified divine agent may not be simple in the sense relevant to probability.
Require theism to provide discriminating expectations rather than unrestricted compatibility with possible observations or merely general explanatory coverage.
Test whether the extent and distribution of severe suffering are compatible with the purposes and obligations attributed to a perfectly good and omnipotent creator.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the proposed personal cause to address its fit with established causal knowledge, evolutionary explanation, and physical accounts of space and time.
Examine whether an independently created immaterial component coheres with evolutionary development, embodied cognition, and the biological cost of the human brain.

sections.title: Personal, physical, and purposive explanation
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether divine agency belongs to a defensible explanatory category and whether the proposed contrast with physical causation is sufficiently complete to support the wider inference.

sections.title: Simplicity as a guide to explanatory probability
sections.rationale: The motion expressly links simplicity with probability, making the meaning, justification, and limits of simplicity central to the comparison between theism and alternative hypotheses.

sections.title: Predicting order, life, consciousness, and agency
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the proposed divine nature generates substantive expectations for the universe's general features and whether those expectations distinguish theism from rival accounts.

sections.title: Divine attributes, physical coherence, and human nature
sections.rationale: Questions about temporality, knowledge, unlimited power, souls, evolution, and embodiment bear on whether the explanatory hypothesis is coherent and appropriately connected to the phenomena invoked.

sections.title: Suffering, moral freedom, and posthumous compensation
sections.rationale: Severe and unevenly distributed suffering is major apparent counterevidence to a perfectly good creator, while freedom, victim benefit, and compensation supply the corresponding reconciliatory requirements.

routes.description: Establish the four claimed historical facts from early Christian materials, connect them as a cumulative evidential set, and show that divine resurrection explains that set more adequately than the proposed literary, visionary, or sociological alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant burial, an empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples’ resurrection belief, and if God raising Jesus provides the best comparative explanation of those facts despite objections from historical analogy and source criticism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest Christian sources establish all four specified facts and that God raising Jesus best explains their conjunction.

centralBridges.description: Establish an identifiable burial and the subsequent discovery of an empty tomb from sufficiently early, independent, and historically credible traditions.
Establish that individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus after his death using authentic early testimony and historically usable narrative sources.
Explain why the earliest disciples sincerely adopted a specific resurrection belief despite the crucifixion and the surrounding Jewish expectations.
Demonstrate comparatively that divine resurrection accounts for the combined evidence better than legendary development, cultural borrowing, visions, or belief-preservation mechanisms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the authenticity, early dating, and historical admissibility of Pauline traditions and the relevant Gospel materials.
Show that proposed pagan and hero-story parallels lack the relevant similarity or causal connection needed to explain the earliest Christian claims.

routes.description: Deny that the surviving sources warrant the four asserted facts or the resurrection inference by applying historical analogy, literary and textual criticism, and ordinary mechanisms for visionary reports, legendary narratives, and the persistence of religious belief.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if material uncertainty remains about one or more foundational facts, or if familiar literary, cultural, visionary, or sociological processes provide sufficient alternatives to prevent divine resurrection from being established as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest sources do not establish the complete factual conjunction or do not make divine resurrection its best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: Show that the burial, empty-tomb, and appearance materials are literary, redactional, or textually uncertain enough that the asserted events are not established.
Use comparable ancient vanished-body, apotheosis, dying-and-rising, and appearance narratives to support a legendary or hagiographic account of the traditions.
Provide non-resurrection pathways for exaltation, appearance reports, and continuing faith, including visions, retrojection, syncretism, and cognitive-dissonance reduction.
Show that invoking divine action does not resolve uncertain historical claims or outperform ordinary explanations under a case-by-case evidential method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend historical ideal-type comparison as requiring meaningful structural similarity rather than exact correspondence or direct literary copying.
Limit the evidential reach of Pauline authenticity claims, later disciple traditions, scholarly consensus, and extra-biblical notices.

sections.title: Source Proximity, Textual Integrity, and Historical Method
sections.rationale: The motion depends on whether Pauline and Gospel materials can function as early historical evidence. This section covers their dating, textual integrity, literary character, admissibility, and the role of analogy in evaluating extraordinary ancient claims.

sections.title: Burial Tradition and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: A known burial place and the subsequent absence of Jesus’ body form a linked evidential foundation for the bodily-resurrection case, while source criticism and alternative literary explanations contest whether either event is historically established.

sections.title: Nature and Historical Status of the Postmortem Appearances
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of individuals and groups are a principal fact asserted by the motion. Their provenance, visionary or bodily character, and relationship to comparable ancient narratives determine what they can establish historically.

sections.title: Origins of the Disciples’ Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: The debate must explain why resurrection belief arose and persisted among Jesus’ followers. Jewish expectations and claimed transformation bear on one account, while syncretism, belief development, and cognitive dissonance supply competing mechanisms.

sections.title: Resurrection as the Best Explanation
sections.rationale: Even if some underlying facts are granted, the motion requires a comparative inference to divine resurrection. This section addresses explanatory adequacy, prior probability, the likelihood of the evidence under alternatives, and whether miraculous agency completes that inference.

routes.description: Establish that theism provides a more adequate unified account of scientific intelligibility, reliable cognition, objective moral obligation, apparent order, and the broader context of suffering than skeptical naturalism provides.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its account connects theism to the principal scientific, epistemic, moral, and explanatory facts while answering naturalistic mechanisms, evidential objections, religious plurality, and the challenge from evil without relying on a merely unexplained gap.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined scientific, moral, and explanatory considerations support theism more strongly than skeptical naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Explain why an orderly and mathematically intelligible universe, truth-directed cognition, and the value of inquiry are expected under a rational creator.
Ground objective moral status and obligation in theism while distinguishing normative authority from evolved feelings or social conditioning.
Defend divine agency as an explanation of established order and functional organization rather than an inference confined to temporary ignorance.
Reconcile suffering with theism or show that the objection requires moral and eschatological premises that the theistic account can coherently supply.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect the historical emergence of modern science to theological commitments about an ordered, knowable, and worthwhile creation.
Specify what observations or comparative explanations may count for theism despite alternative natural or advanced-agent interpretations.

routes.description: Establish that public evidence, testable natural mechanisms, and empirically informed morality explain the relevant phenomena without a divine hypothesis, while suffering and underdetermination count against traditional theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if natural inquiry remains adequate for science, cognition, origins, design, and morality; if proposed divine explanations lack discriminating support or specificity; and if theism does not resolve the evidential challenge posed by innocent suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that the relevant evidence and explanatory methods support skeptical naturalism at least more strongly than the proposed theistic account.

centralBridges.description: Require publicly reproducible, discriminating evidence and causal mechanisms before treating supernatural agency as an explanation.
Account for apparent design, cognitive reliability, and possible cosmic origins through testable or provisionally investigated natural processes.
Explain moral knowledge and obligation through facts about sentient flourishing, reciprocity, cooperation, reasoning, and empirically studied human nature.
Establish the evidential tension between extensive preventable innocent suffering and a deity possessing perfect goodness and unlimited power.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate scientific validity from the religious identity of early investigators and address the specificity problem created by competing religions.
Identify how unfalsifiable qualifications, asymmetric attribution, or appeals to unknown causes limit the explanatory content of the God hypothesis.

sections.title: Scientific Intelligibility, Cognition, and Historical Origins
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the order of nature, human access to truth, the value of inquiry, and the historical rise of science receive a distinctive theistic explanation or are adequately grounded by universal scientific practice and evolved cognition.

sections.title: Design, Cosmic Origins, and Natural Mechanisms
sections.rationale: This issue covers the competing explanations for functional complexity and cosmic origins, including divine agency, evolutionary processes, causal regress concerns, unsettled cosmology, and the permissibility of withholding conclusions while inquiry continues.

sections.title: Evidence, Falsifiability, and Explanatory Method
sections.rationale: This issue determines what could discriminate supernatural agency from natural or advanced-agent alternatives, whether theistic explanation supplies causal content, and whether either framework improperly fixes its conclusion regardless of possible observations.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Human Moral Status
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether moral truth and binding obligation require divine grounding or can arise from reason, reciprocity, flourishing, cooperation, moral psychology, and social inquiry, including the distinction between explaining moral beliefs and justifying them.

sections.title: Evil, Innocent Suffering, and Theistic Coherence
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether preventable innocent suffering conflicts with a perfectly good and powerful God, whether the objection presupposes objective moral standards, and whether a wider theistic account of suffering and death changes that conflict.

moves.attributionBasis: Wood remains the announced opening speaker and presents a sustained historical argument supported by attributed statements from named scientists.

routes.description: Establish a likelihood comparison in which life-permitting fine-tuning is substantially more expected given classical perfect-being theism than given the complete admissible space of single-universe naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it grounds the fine-tuning datum, supplies a defensible expectation of valuable conscious life under perfect-being theism, and shows that hypothesis augmentation, simulation, aggregated alternatives, and naturalistic parsimony do not erase the comparative evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that the posterior-confirming force of fine-tuning remains strong after the relevant theistic and naturalistic hypothesis spaces are compared.

centralBridges.description: Establish that life-permitting conditions are far less expected under single-universe naturalism than under a perfectly good creator with reasons to value conscious moral life.
Explain why admissible alien, simulation, time-travel, or fine-tuning-specific naturalistic alternatives do not collectively neutralize the likelihood asymmetry.
Justify an intrinsic-probability treatment under which the coherence or simplicity of perfect-being theism offsets the specificity of augmented naturalistic rivals.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a principled basis for empirical evidence to discriminate between theism and broad naturalistic alternatives despite logical compatibility with multiple causes.
Account for naturalism's ontological economy and explain how it should be balanced against the claimed conditional-probability advantage.

routes.description: Undercut the strong-evidence inference by challenging the specification and aggregation of the rival hypothesis spaces, the predictive content of divine psychology, and the status of apparent fine-tuning as an objective datum.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism cannot be assigned a sufficiently reliable likelihood advantage over the full naturalistic alternative space, or if uncertainty about priors, divine intentions, or the fine-tuning datum prevents the asserted strong confirmation.

motionBridge.description: Show that fine-tuning does not strongly discriminate in favor of God once hypothesis-space ambiguity and uncertain theistic predictions are included.

centralBridges.description: Require comparison with the aggregated space of admissible naturalistic explanations rather than with a selectively austere naturalistic hypothesis.
Establish that perfect goodness and other divine attributes do not yield sufficiently determinate predictions about creating life-permitting conditions.
Show that aggregation, modesty, coherence, and ontological parsimony leave the relevant intrinsic-probability comparison unresolved.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Demonstrate how apparently purposive or religious evidence can remain compatible with broad naturalistic agency explanations.
Test whether apparent fine-tuning is an objective feature requiring explanation or instead a sign that the operative physical theory is defective.

sections.title: The Fine-Tuning Datum and the Core Likelihood Comparison
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational issue: whether life-permitting parameters constitute an objective and improbable datum whose likelihood differs substantially between classical theism and single-universe naturalism.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and the Relevant Comparison Class
sections.rationale: The strength of the inference depends on whether theism must outperform one austere naturalistic hypothesis or the aggregated space of alien, simulation, time-travel, and other admissible naturalistic explanations.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Agency, and Predictive Expectations
sections.rationale: A likelihood advantage for theism requires a defensible bridge from perfect divine goodness to the creation of valuable conscious life, while the opposing burden tests whether divine intentions remain too indeterminate.

sections.title: Intrinsic Probability, Coherence, Modesty, and Parsimony
sections.rationale: This issue determines how the prior plausibility of perfect-being theism compares with disjunctions of limited or augmented naturalistic hypotheses before the fine-tuning evidence is incorporated.

sections.title: Empirical Discrimination and Religious Ambiguity
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether broad alternative explanations make empirical evidence persistently ambiguous and whether such ambiguity undercuts fine-tuning without foreclosing every possible non-empirical argument concerning God.

routes.description: Establish that finite, composite beings exhibit real essence, form, and received existence, requiring an external self-existent ground that accounts for their unity, diversity, and actuality and can be identified with the God of classical theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective essences and essence-existence composition are established, the required ground is shown to be necessary and external to contingent reality, and the inference reaches classical theism rather than an unspecified cause.

motionBridge.description: Show that the necessary self-existent ground inferred from contingent composition possesses the identity required by the God of classical theism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that form or essence is an objective feature of beings and is not exhausted by physical description, classification, language, or assigned use.
Establish a real distinction in finite beings between what they are and the act by which they exist, requiring an account of their conjunction.
Show that the unity of diverse parts and the composition of essence with existence require an external composing ground rather than an unexplained natural arrangement.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Justify metaphysical reasoning about reality as a whole as an appropriate method for reaching conclusions unavailable from piecemeal empirical inquiry alone.
Specify how historical claims, reported miracles, prediction, explanatory scope, and personal experience could support identification of the necessary ground with a revealed God.

routes.description: Show that the proposed essence, composition, and necessary-ground claims lack independent demonstration and do not discriminate a divine agent from physical, descriptive, unknown, or non-agent explanations, leaving the classical-theist conclusion evidentially unwarranted.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the pro premises remain unsupported or adequately explained without additional metaphysical entities, the inference from grounding to agency or classical theism fails, and revelation or experience does not supply independently sufficient evidence.

motionBridge.description: Show that the presented considerations do not provide testable, independently supported, and discriminating evidence for the God of classical theism.

centralBridges.description: Require claims about God and metaphysical entities to receive support proportionate to their background plausibility and capable of distinguishing them from alternatives.
Account for identity, classification, form, and natural arrangement through physical properties, causal continuity, and human abstractions without positing independently existing essences.
Show that a need for explanation or causal grounding does not by itself establish intentional composition, a personal agent, or the God of classical theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Begin from observed beings and acknowledged uncertainty without classifying them as created or placing God among live explanations absent independent support.
Test claims of revelation and divine presence against sincere nonbelief, conflicting interpretation, and the apparent absence of clear universal disclosure.

sections.title: Metaphysical Method and Evidential Standards
sections.rationale: Determines whether reasoning about being as a whole can constitute good evidence and what independent support, testability, background knowledge, or explanatory discrimination the motion requires.

sections.title: Essence, Form, Identity, and Abstraction
sections.rationale: Addresses whether objective essences or forms exist beyond physical properties, causal continuity, classifications, linguistic concepts, intended functions, and changing material arrangements.

sections.title: Essence-Existence Composition and the Necessary Ground
sections.rationale: Covers the principal affirmative inference from finite beings whose essence and existence are distinct to a self-existent ground, together with objections to its premises and inferential validity.

sections.title: Composition, Causation, and the Inference to Agency
sections.rationale: Tests whether unity, diversity, parts, and observed effects require an external composer or personal cause, or whether that step assumes agency without discriminating evidence.

sections.title: From a Ground of Being to Classical Theism
sections.rationale: Examines whether the proposed necessary ground is adequately identified with the God of classical theism through philosophical identity claims, historical revelation, reported miracles, experience, and the challenge of divine hiddenness.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Rhodes, and the uninterrupted answer continues until the moderator closes the turn.

components.text: Whether the transition from finite or accidental existence to a per-se self-existent ground has an articulated logical principle.
Whether a self-declared metaphysical principle supplies the independent evidential warrant missing from the burnt-wood analogy.

response.rationale: The reply supplies the per-accidens-to-per-se principle as an answer to the missing-bridge challenge, but it does not defend applying that principle to existence itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive missing inference but leaves both the category application and independent warrant unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended entailment is recoverable, but accidental existence shifts from predication by analogy to a universal ontological status.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The principle is called self-evident and undeniable despite the unsupported transfer from accidental properties such as tallness to existence.

charity.alternative: Finite beings may exist dependently without existence being an accident inhering in a self-existent substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: The tallness analogy does not show that existence is the same kind of accidental predicate or that one per-se bearer follows.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (57 and 53); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The tallness analogy illustrates per-accidens predication but does not independently warrant a unique self-existent ontological ground.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the essence-existence composition bridge and answers a central justificatory challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (61 and 58); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rhodes invokes the scholastic principle that per accidens implies per se, analogizing accidental existence to tallness inhering in a substance.

moves.speaker: Kenny Rhodes
moves.proposition: A claimed divine revelation can be assessed through historical documents, miracle reports, fulfilled prediction, and explanatory scope concerning origin, meaning, morality, and destiny.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty asks Rhodes how revelation could be recognized, and Rhodes gives the complete answer before the moderator moves to another question.

components.text: Whether purported divine revelation has publicly assessable indicators beyond private conviction or ambiguous personal experience.
Whether historical revelation could provide the additional evidence needed to identify an abstract ground with a revealed God.

response.rationale: The reply specifies public historical and explanatory tests for revelation, contacting both evidential accessibility and identification, though it supplies no test results.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it gives relevant verification criteria but does not answer why clear disclosure remains absent or show that any revelation passes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly presents historical documents, prediction, miracles, and explanatory scope as proposed tests rather than established successes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that revelation can be assessed by these criteria is appropriately distinguished from claiming that Christianity has passed them.

charity.alternative: Historical texts and reported predictions may remain ambiguous, dependent, or compatible with nondivine explanations.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move proposes tests but does not yet establish independence, authenticity, fulfilled prediction, or divine discrimination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed sequence from treating texts historically to evaluating predictions and explanatory scope is coherent and appropriately conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (68 and 71); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supports the revelation-and-experience bridge and reaches the top of that range.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer fairly treats revelation as assessable evidence while leaving the skeptical verification and alternative-explanation demands open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rhodes proposes treating biblical materials as historical documents and testing prophecy, miracles, and explanatory scope before attributing divine inspiration.

moves.speaker: Kenny Rhodes
moves.proposition: The inference from a necessary creator to the Christian God is philosophical rather than empirical because piecemeal examination of parts cannot resolve the nature of reality as a whole.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is explicitly addressed to Rhodes, and the short first-person answer ends before he shifts to explaining his physical condition.

components.text: Whether the inference to the Christian God has adequate independently supported and discriminating evidence given its background plausibility.
Whether philosophical reasoning supplies the missing identity bridge from necessary creator to the specifically Christian God.
Whether empirical examination of parts is methodologically sufficient for questions about reality as a whole.

response.rationale: The reply reiterates a methodological limit on empirical inquiry, but it neither supplies the requested identity argument nor addresses background support and discrimination for Christianity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, the whole-versus-parts point bears on method but leaves the decisive evidential and identification demands uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological contrast is recoverable, but empirical evidence, philosophical inference, parts, and whole lack clarifying boundaries.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical denial that empirical evidence can be given does not establish that the proposed philosophical route reaches Christianity.

charity.alternative: The evidential challenge allows philosophical evidence if it independently supports and discriminates the Christian conclusion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Labeling the inference philosophical does not answer whether its premises identify Christianity rather than another ground or explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The answer states a method distinction but does not derive the Christian identity or explain why empirical information cannot bear on it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No philosophical premises, historical evidence, or discriminating bridge is supplied in this short rejection of empirical evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it attacks the con evidential standard by denying empirical applicability, though only at the lower end.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (58 and 56); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

moves.evidenceBasis: Rhodes says he cannot give empirical evidence because examining reality part by part cannot explain the nature of the whole.

routes.description: Establish that religious belief better secures moral knowledge and social judgment by grounding durable duties in divine authority and by showing that religious traditions can identify grave public evils more reliably than secular institutions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine authorship is given an adequate basis, transcendent authority explains the stability of binding duties, and the practical record supports religion's comparative capacity to recognize evil and sustain a good society.

motionBridge.description: Show that divine authority provides a firmer basis for moral knowledge and recognition of social evil than secular ethical deliberation provides.

centralBridges.description: Provide grounds for believing in an intentional creator and for treating sacred teaching as a credible source of moral authority.
Explain why divine authority makes core prohibitions binding and durable despite fallible human preferences and disagreement.
Show that a worldview's moral adequacy is tested by its capacity to identify major evils and contribute to a good society.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how disputed ancient rules may represent moral advances when interpreted within their historical setting.
Support the comparative claim that religious communities can recognize ideologically motivated evil that secular institutions overlook.

routes.description: Establish that secular ethical realism can guide moral knowledge and progress through evidence about conscious experience, rational inquiry, cooperation, and revisable public reasoning without relying on supernatural authorship or sacred authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if wellbeing and suffering furnish defensible moral facts, rational inquiry explains moral convergence and correction, and religious dogma is shown to be unnecessary or obstructive in identifying and remedying social evil.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular ethical realism can ground moral knowledge and moral progress without supernatural premises or sacred texts.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral distinctions in facts about the happiness, suffering, capacities, and relationships of conscious creatures.
Explain how open-ended rational inquiry can discover, test, and revise moral rules while distinguishing evidence-based realism from pragmatism.
Show how unsupported supernatural or political dogmas can motivate violence and obstruct effective moral judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how attachment, reciprocity, mutual care, and viable social cooperation support prohibitions such as the rule against murder.
Show how secular analysis can make morally relevant distinctions among forms and stages of conscious life.

sections.title: Moral Authority and Binding Obligation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether durable moral duties require divine command or can arise from rationally accessible facts about persons, cooperation, harm, and flourishing.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge and Ethical Realism
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require an account of how moral claims become knowable, objective, corrigible, and distinguishable from preference or mere practical success.

sections.title: Creator, Scripture, and Dogmatic Authority
sections.rationale: The status of a creator and sacred texts matters because the pro route invokes them as foundations while the con route challenges their evidentiary basis and moral reliability.

sections.title: Recognizing Social Evil and Testing Worldviews
sections.rationale: The debate uses communism, fascism, religious extremism, and institutional judgment to test which framework better identifies dangerous ideologies and supports moral progress.

sections.title: Consciousness, Human Status, and Contested Cases
sections.rationale: Disputes involving human uniqueness, animals, embryos, fetuses, suffering, and development test how each framework draws and justifies morally significant boundaries.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Claims that sacred books were written or informed by a supernatural creator are unsupported and dangerously divisive, particularly because they obstruct rational responses to religious extremism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager directly invites Harris to characterize his view, and Harris delivers the ensuing first-person explanation without attribution ambiguity.

response.rationale: This is a constructive challenge to supernatural authorship and its alleged harmful consequences, so no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a central challenge but compresses the evidentiary support for its broad consequences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but claims about divisiveness, danger, and the Muslim world broaden beyond the specifically stated supernatural premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt confidently calls the dogma uniquely dangerous and unsupported without supplying comparative evidence for that breadth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unsupported supernatural authorship to dangerous divisiveness is intelligible but leaves a material causal bridge underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (58 and 60); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central dogma-and-harm bridge, though it does not complete the broader secular-grounding route.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is examined closely enough for a meaningful charity test in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly labels supernatural scriptural authorship unsupported, divisive, dangerous, and costly in relation to the Muslim world.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Religious Americans are more likely than secular academics to recognize the threat of Islamic totalitarianism, supporting a comparative claim that religiosity can sharpen rather than impede the identification of grave social evil.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly speaks in the first person, identifies himself among religious Americans, and develops the challenge addressed to Harris.

components.text: Whether religion obstructs recognition of religious extremism and its associated social danger.
Whether supernatural scriptural claims themselves are evidentially supported.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the claimed practical obstruction by alleging superior religious recognition of Islamic totalitarianism, but it does not answer the unsupported-authorship component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that reaches the decisive practical-harm component while leaving the supernatural-evidence challenge untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is clear, but categories such as evangelical leaders, secular professors, and religious Americans shift without a stated sampling scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A broad comparative likelihood is asserted from an acknowledged example without documentation, base rates, or qualification about populations.

charity.alternative: Harris can oppose supernatural dogma while conceding that some religious observers recognize Islamist threats accurately.
charity.decisiveQualification: That concession would not establish that religiosity generally improves recognition of social evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (77 and 73); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The population comparison and designation of the greatest moral threat are asserted without representative evidence or rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports religious discernment, a subsidiary bridge, and does so near the upper part of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager identifies a genuine tension in the practical claim, though he overextends a bounded concession into a broad comparative conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager contrasts evangelical Christian leaders with secular academic professors in recognizing Islamic totalitarianism as a major threat.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: When martyrdom, jihad, and immediate paradise are accepted as true religious premises, catastrophic violence can be internally rational, and religious believers may recognize that motivational logic particularly clearly.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris begins with an explicit concession and then explains, in a continuous response, why religious observers recognize the motivating beliefs.

components.text: Why religious observers may recognize Islamist totalitarian danger more readily.
Whether the asserted religious-versus-secular recognition frequency is empirically established.
Whether recognition of this threat demonstrates religion's broader comparative moral adequacy.

response.rationale: Harris justifies replacing the inference from recognition to religious moral superiority with an explanation based on familiarity with religious motivation, preserving the recognition issue while defeating its proposed consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it explicitly explains the observed recognition while showing why that observation does not support the broader comparative inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on accepting martyrdom, jihad, and paradise premises, keeping its terms and inferential scope stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The strong conclusion is framed conditionally: given the specified metaphysical premises, violent conduct can be instrumentally rational.

charity.alternative: Religious Americans identify a real Islamist threat that secular academics may underestimate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Accurate threat recognition does not show that religion is the superior cause when religious premises also explain the threat's motivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The means-end inference is clear and valid once the stated beliefs about martyrdom and immediate paradise are conditionally granted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (73 and 72); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central dogma-and-harm bridge by explaining how religious premises can internally rationalize catastrophic violence.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris grants the recognition point and supplies a stronger competing explanation that directly limits its value for Prager's comparative conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies martyrdom, jihad, and paradise as premises under which dying in defense of faith becomes instrumentally rational.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Whether religion has evidentiary support is distinct from the practical moral question of which worldview is more likely to produce a good society, a test on which anti-religious secular institutions allegedly failed by overlooking communism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager interrupts to distinguish evidentiary questions from social consequences and then expressly states the comparative argument he is advancing.

components.text: Whether the practical moral performance of a worldview should be assessed separately from evidence for religion.
Whether supernatural authorship claims are adequately supported by evidence.
Whether specified religious premises can make violent conduct internally rational.

response.rationale: Prager expressly separates evidentiary support from the preserved practical issue of producing a good society, justifying that replacement demand while leaving the original evidentiary and motivational claims unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The justified reframe preserves a legitimate comparative moral-performance issue and answers it, though the communism example remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence and practical performance is clear, but good world and anti-religious secular world remain broad and underqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the anti-religious secular world a moral failure on communism exceeds the single asserted historical comparison supplied here.

charity.alternative: A worldview may be evidentially unsupported even if some adherents identify particular social evils correctly.
charity.decisiveQualification: Practical success is relevant to comparative moral adequacy but cannot substitute for the creator-and-scripture evidentiary burden.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (79 and 78); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (56 and 58); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely supports the central social-evil test by proposing practical moral performance as a criterion for worldview assessment.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager fairly distinguishes two questions, but his practical reframe risks sidelining rather than resolving the foundational evidentiary challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager explicitly distinguishes evidence for religion from producing a good world and cites secular institutions' alleged failure regarding communism.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Atheism was not the operative cause of communist, Nazi, or Khmer Rouge atrocities; closed political dogma was the common danger, while open-ended rational inquiry offers a general corrective to unjustified belief.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris rejects the proposed diagnosis, names political dogma as the relevant cause, and answers Prager's direct question about grounding the prohibition on murder.

components.text: Whether atheism or anti-religious secularism is the operative cause of totalitarian atrocities.
Whether secular institutions historically failed to recognize communism as evil.
Whether religious Americans comparatively recognize Islamic totalitarian threats better.

response.rationale: Harris expressly rejects atheism as the diagnosis, identifies closed political dogma as the operative defect, and states open-ended rational inquiry as the corrective consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly attacks the decisive causal inference and supplies a general alternative diagnosis, placing it high within diagnostic defeats.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal contrast is clear, although dogma across the board and rational people are broad terms whose institutional scope is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical rejection of atheism as the problem exceeds the excerpt's comparative evidence, though the common-dogma diagnosis is clearly articulated.

charity.alternative: Atheistic or anti-religious commitments materially caused communist and other totalitarian atrocities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Political dogma can coexist with atheism, so correlation alone does not identify atheism as the operative cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (86 and 84); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (70 and 68); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central open-inquiry bridge by contrasting closed dogma with revisable rational inquiry as a corrective.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately engages the causal alternative and supplies the decisive distinction, though it does not examine mixed causal contributions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris rejects atheism as the cause of communist, Nazi, and Khmer Rouge evil and instead identifies closed political dogma.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The existence of persons capable of conversation, together with the existence and apparent design of the world, makes an intentional creator more plausible than treating human and cosmic existence as sheer coincidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager answers Harris's direct question about his belief and supplies a clearly personal, sustained inference from existence and design to a creator.

components.text: Whether there are grounds for believing that an intentional creator exists.
Whether any particular sacred book was written or informed by that creator.
Whether open-ended inquiry corrects unjustified political or religious belief.

response.rationale: The design inference contacts the creator-evidence component of Harris's challenge, but it gives no bridge from a creator to any sacred text and does not address open inquiry.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts a decisive creator component but leaves the scripture-authorship and dogmatic-harm components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The creator inference is recoverable, but coincidence, coming about on its own, creation, and design are treated as interchangeable alternatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that non-design is almost absurd sharply exceeds the supplied observation of existence and omits naturalistic alternatives.

charity.alternative: Human and cosmic existence may arise through nonintentional natural processes rather than sheer coincidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting intentional design does not require treating every causal process as an unexplained pure coincidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (58 and 61); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Existence and apparent design are invoked without defending the design judgment or comparing naturalistic causal explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies purported grounds for an intentional creator, placing it high within the central creator-and-scripture tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (55 and 59); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager argues from human conversation, worldly existence, and apparent design to a creator while characterizing coincidence as intellectually absurd.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The prohibition on murder remains durable because it rests on divine authority, whereas reliance on discussion alone places unwarranted confidence in fallible human nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly contrasts his divine-command account with Harris's conversational account and states his judgment about their relative rationality.

components.text: Whether open-ended rational discussion can ground and preserve the prohibition on murder.

routes.description: Establish Christianity through a cumulative public-evidence case in which historically grounded testimony and its theological setting support Jesus's bodily resurrection, while biblical teaching remains compatible with divine goodness and authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available historical evidence makes bodily resurrection the best explanation, the surrounding theological context connects that event to Jesus's identity and Christian claims, and the principal reliability and moral-authority objections can be reconciled with Christianity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative resurrection, identity, reliability, and moral-authority case to the conclusion that Christianity is true and warrants rational commitment.

centralBridges.description: Establish historically grounded resurrection appearances and related facts for which bodily resurrection is the best cumulative explanation.
Establish that the Gospel and apostolic materials are sufficiently early, interlocking, and reliable to support the historical premises.
Show that Jesus's scriptural and theological setting raises the resurrection hypothesis's credibility and connects resurrection to his identity and authority.
Reconcile challenged biblical laws, narratives, and doctrines with the goodness and moral authority attributed to the Christian God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply an evidential framework under which sufficiently strong evidence can overcome a low prior probability for a supernatural explanation.
Explain Christian faith as trust grounded in evidence and prior reasons rather than belief adopted independently of evidence.

routes.description: Withhold acceptance of Christianity by challenging the adequacy and independence of its resurrection sources, denying the inference from resurrection to the wider religion, and presenting biblical teaching and Christian doctrine as incompatible with credible moral authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the resurrection case does not meet its required evidential burden, if resurrection would not establish Christianity's further identity and authority claims, or if independent moral objections defeat the claimed authority or warranted allegiance of Christianity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical, theological, and moral premises offered do not jointly establish Christianity as true or authoritative.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, disputed, internally divergent, or literarily shaped sources are insufficient to establish an extraordinary bodily resurrection.
Demonstrate that even a resurrection would not by itself establish Jesus's divinity, moral authority, Christian doctrine, or a duty of allegiance.
Show that challenged biblical laws, narratives, and doctrines conflict with the perfect goodness required for divine moral authority.
Challenge prophecy and theological context as independent grounds for raising the prior credibility of Jesus's resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge whether the evidence about apostolic suffering and death establishes sincere, recantable testimony to bodily resurrection.
Require an account of morally significant animal suffering that is compatible with the agency and goodness of the Christian God.

sections.title: Resurrection Appearances and Competing Historical Explanations
sections.rationale: The existence, character, and sincerity of reported appearances supply the principal historical basis for resurrection, while the evidential threshold and availability of non-resurrection explanations determine whether that basis can bear the central historical burden.

sections.title: Gospel Reliability, Corroboration, and Narrative Construction
sections.rationale: The resurrection inference depends on whether Gospel and apostolic materials function as historically grounded testimony; alleged contradictions, literary parallels, interlocking details, and inductive reliability therefore form a distinct source-level clash.

sections.title: Prior Probability, Prophecy, and the Bridge to Christianity
sections.rationale: This issue governs both whether a supernatural resurrection can become credible in Jesus's theological setting and whether such an event would establish divinity, doctrinal truth, moral authority, or warranted allegiance to Christianity.

sections.title: Biblical Teaching, Atonement, and Divine Moral Authority
sections.rationale: Biblical slavery texts, conquest narratives, salvation and atonement doctrines, and the basis of divine-command morality provide an independent motion-level test of whether Christianity can credibly claim a perfectly good and authoritative source.

sections.title: Suffering, Evidence, and Rational Christian Commitment
sections.rationale: Animal suffering tests the compatibility of Christian theism with divine goodness, while disputes about faith, evidential responsibility, and conditional importance address what would rationally support further inquiry or commitment.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the better explanation by connecting objective morality, trustworthy rational agency, consciousness, and freedom to a divine personal ground while showing that theism can accommodate the evidential challenges from suffering, cosmic conditions, and nonbelief.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its positive divine-grounding account jointly explains the principal mental, moral, and epistemic phenomena and its auxiliary theological explanations make the principal naturalistic evidence insufficient to overturn that comparative case.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christian theism provides the more unified and adequate explanation of the motion's moral, epistemic, mental, agential, and evidential phenomena.

centralBridges.description: Connect objective moral truth, obligation, and the intelligibility of evil to a necessary personal transcendent ground.
Explain reliable cognition, rational inference, responsibility, and meaningful freedom through purposive agency rather than unguided adaptive causation alone.
Account for irreducible finite consciousness through an ultimate divine consciousness and an immaterial dimension of persons.
Supply theistically coherent reasons why animal suffering, cosmic hostility, and nonresistant nonbelief may occur despite divine goodness and love.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether naturalistic additions for morality and consciousness preserve the simplicity and unity claimed for that worldview.
Relate fine-tuning, cosmic habitability conditions, restoration, soul-building, and divine hiddenness to the broader purposive account.

routes.description: Establish atheistic naturalism as the better explanation by combining its comparative simplicity with naturalistic accounts of morality, cognition, consciousness, and freedom, while treating animal suffering, cosmic hostility, and nonresistant nonbelief as evidence more expected without a perfectly good and loving creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalism accommodates the positive phenomena without requiring a divine ground and if the observed patterns of suffering, cosmic inhospitability, and sincere nonbelief remain materially more congruent with indifferent natural processes than with Christian theism.

motionBridge.description: Show that atheistic naturalism explains the full evidential pattern with fewer fundamental commitments and without the tensions generated by a perfect divine creator.

centralBridges.description: Provide naturalistic resources for objective morality, reliable cognition, irreducible consciousness, reasons-responsive freedom, and rational agency.
Show why the scale, history, and predatory organization of nonmoral animal suffering are expected under indifferent evolution but require substantive explanation under theism.
Connect cosmic hostility and the distribution of nonresistant nonbelief to naturalistic expectations while identifying their tension with divine purpose and perfect love.
Test whether appeals to the fall, freedom, soul-building, compensation, hiddenness, and divine moral grounding explain the specific phenomena rather than merely permitting them.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Apply qualitative simplicity while allowing evidentially motivated fundamental phenomenal or normative features within naturalism.
Examine the compatibility of Molinism with libertarian freedom and the objectivity of morality grounded in a divine person.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Divine Grounding, and Evil
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether moral truth, authority, teleology, and the classification of evil require a necessary personal ground or can exist as irreducible normative facts without God.

sections.title: Knowledge, Rationality, and Evolutionary Determination
sections.rationale: The comparative case depends on whether unguided evolution and causal determination undermine trustworthy cognition or can generate reliable, content-sensitive, reasons-responsive belief formation.

sections.title: Consciousness, Freedom, and Explanatory Simplicity
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether irreducible consciousness and meaningful agency require souls and an ultimate mind, or fit a naturalistic account with fundamental phenomenal properties and compatibilist freedom.

sections.title: Animal Suffering, Predation, and Theodicy
sections.rationale: The long history and organized forms of nonmoral suffering create a major comparative test between indifferent evolution and theistic explanations involving freedom, the fall, soul-building, restoration, or compensation.

sections.title: Cosmic Hostility, Fine-Tuning, and Habitability
sections.rationale: The universe's limited hospitality to embodied moral life must be weighed against fine-tuning, the functional role of cosmic scale and emptiness, and competing expectations about divine creative purpose.

sections.title: Nonresistant Nonbelief and Perfect Divine Love
sections.rationale: The existence and distribution of sincere nonbelief test whether perfect love requires accessible relationship with God or permits hiddenness for protective, developmental, or relational purposes.

routes.description: Establish that religions and concepts of God are products of cultural evolution and human design, while showing that cosmology, apparent design, consciousness, morality, and social value admit naturalistic accounts that do not require a supernatural creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the human-development account explains religious concepts and the principal phenomena offered for theism can be understood without treating a divine creator as the necessary or preferable explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historical and cultural evolution of God concepts to the conclusion that they are human constructions rather than discoveries of a real supernatural creator.

centralBridges.description: Provide bottom-up natural explanations for apparent design, consciousness, agency, and morality without presupposing a superior originating mind.
Show that cosmic beginnings and life-permitting conditions do not entail divine causation and that invoking a creator leaves substantial explanatory demands unresolved.
Ground moral development and social cooperation in human capacities, shared inquiry, and revisable institutions rather than continuing supernatural authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why publicly testable and self-correcting inquiry can examine religious, experiential, and consciousness claims without granting them automatic supernatural significance.
Account for religion's persistence and historical social contributions while distinguishing those functions from evidence that its supernatural claims are true.

routes.description: Establish that a real divine creator offers a unified explanation for the universe's beginning and order, life-permitting conditions, rational consciousness, free agency, morality, and religious experience, while showing that human formation of religious concepts does not imply an unreal referent.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the convergent cosmological, experiential, mental, and moral considerations provide rational support for divine reality and withstand the claim that cultural evolution or naturalistic explanation makes God merely a human invention.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative explanatory case from cosmos, mind, morality, and experience to rational support for a creator existing independently of human concepts.

centralBridges.description: Infer an explanatory ground beyond nature from the beginning, lawful order, and life-permitting structure of the universe.
Show that consciousness, rational understanding, intentional choice, and responsibility are not adequately exhausted by deterministic material processes.
Explain objective moral commitments, human dignity, and substantial altruism through a transcendent foundation that secular inheritance alone may not sustain.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend religious experience and other subjectively accessed realities as potentially rational evidence despite limits on direct public observation.
Distinguish the human development and disagreement of religious concepts from the separate question whether those concepts refer to an independent reality.

sections.title: Religious Concepts, Cultural Evolution, and Independent Reality
sections.rationale: This issue directly frames the motion: whether the development, variation, and human transmission of religions and God concepts establish invention, or remain compatible with reference to a reality independent of those concepts.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Natural Law, and Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: The universe's beginning, intelligible order, and life-permitting parameters form the principal cosmological case for a creator and the principal clash over anthropic, multiverse, regress, and explanatory alternatives.

sections.title: Consciousness, Reason, Free Will, and Evolutionary Explanation
sections.rationale: Whether consciousness, truth-directed reason, intentional choice, and responsibility can arise through natural processes or require a nonmaterial foundation is a major test of the rival explanatory frameworks.

sections.title: Morality, Human Dignity, and Secular Social Order
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral origins, normative authority, altruism, equality, and the durability of secular institutions bear directly on whether morality supplies rational support for God.

sections.title: Religious Experience, Cognitive Limits, and Epistemic Standards
sections.rationale: This issue determines what evidential status religious experience may have and whether public testing, subjective access, human cognitive limits, disagreement, and parsimony favor or exclude theistic belief.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Religions are human inventions analogous to languages and music: collective cultural products that arise repeatedly and evolve across generations rather than remaining fixed creations.
moves.attributionBasis: The statement occurs within Dennett's uninterrupted opening turn and expressly presents his view of religion.

response.rationale: This is a constructive account of religions as recurrent, evolving human cultural products, so no earlier opposing move supplies a response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes a principal historical-cultural premise of the pro route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cultural-evolution proposition is readily recoverable, though the analogy does not explicitly delimit what follows about independent reality.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Rapid proliferation and evolutionary history support extensive human production, but do not alone establish that every religious referent is invented.

charity.alternative: Religions are human cultural productions in the sense that their institutions, doctrines, and transmission histories are collectively shaped and evolve.
charity.decisiveQualification: Human production of traditions does not by itself prove that every purported supernatural referent is unreal.

moves.speaker: Dinesh D'Souza
moves.proposition: Consciousness, intentional choice, and moral responsibility cannot be adequately reduced to deterministic material processes.
moves.attributionBasis: D'Souza continues the same uninterrupted address, contrasts his position with Dennett's, and uses his own possible actions as examples.

moves.proposition: The beginning of space and time in this universe does not establish divine creation, because positing God merely renews rather than resolves the demand for an origin.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Observers necessarily inhabit a universe compatible with observers, so apparent fine-tuning can be explained through anthropic selection and possible alternative universes without intelligent design.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett continues without interruption and explicitly reframes D'Souza's fine-tuning question through the anthropic principle and possible universes.

components.text: Whether life-permitting cosmic conditions are more simply explained by deliberate creator design.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it expressly contacts the fine-tuning inference and supplies a recognizable competing explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Observer selection necessarily conditions observation, but saying fine-tuning requires no creator explanation depends on an unestablished range of universes or laws.

charity.decisiveQualification: Observer selection alone does not establish the ensemble or explain why life-permitting possibilities exist.

moves.proposition: Darwinian explanations of free will, consciousness, choice, and intentionality cannot be rejected merely by asserting their impossibility when substantive naturalistic explanatory work exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly answers D'Souza's preceding claims and refers to Dennett's own career developing naturalistic explanations of these phenomena.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Dennett explicitly concedes the opponent might be right and claims progress rather than a demonstrated complete explanation, matching the limited support shown.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett

moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly turns to atheism and morality, speaks continuously through the applause boundary, and develops a secular account of moral judgment.
